What does Manuscript Check assess?

It screens abbreviations, references, numbers, units, writing structure, terminology, figures, tables, and equations. Each module applies its own structural exclusions so captions, references, front matter, equations, and other non-prose content are not treated like ordinary sentences.

Add one correctly formatted reference (optional)

Use the CSL library to validate reference formatting against a selected journal or citation style. Core field detection remains independent of CSL rules. Import your CSL ZIP once, select a style, and Manuscript Check will load only that style when needed. Complex CSL branches that cannot be interpreted confidently are left unvalidated rather than guessed.

Search the full Zotero CSL style catalogue, including journal-specific dependent styles. The 2,858-style local ZIP supplies the unique parent formatting rules. A selected style affects formatting validation only; it never changes whether author, year, title, source, volume, pages, or DOI fields are detected.

Checking local CSL library…

The imported ZIP and the searchable style catalogue are stored only in your browser using IndexedDB when available. The catalogue is refreshed from Zotero when internet access is available and then remains searchable offline. The ZIP supplies the unique parent CSL rules; journal-specific dependent styles are resolved to those parent rules.

Journal/style catalogue and CSL rules are based on the open-source Citation Style Language (CSL) project and Zotero Style Repository. CSL styles are distributed under CC BY-SA 3.0.

Your results at a glance

Open the sections below to review findings, manuscript instances, and recommendations.

Recommended workflow: review high-confidence findings first, inspect the manuscript context shown with each finding, then apply a recommendation only when it is scientifically and editorially appropriate.

Check by section

How to read the results

Critical error

High-confidence finding that should normally be addressed.

Review item

Potential inconsistency that needs author judgement or journal-specific checking.

Editorial note

Lower-priority consistency or readability observation.

In ledgers: yes = field found · no = expected field missing · n/a = not required for that item.

Important: Manuscript Check is an editorial screening tool. A highlighted item is something worth checking, not proof that the manuscript is wrong. Scientific meaning and the target journal's instructions take priority.

Abbreviation report

This is a heuristic aid, not a substitute for a careful read. Detection of abbreviations and definitions is pattern-based and can still miss unusual cases. All-caps paper titles and other excluded front matter are not treated as abbreviation sources. Definitions are recognised from both conventional acronym expansions and scientific notation introduced semantically, such as "BET surface area (SBET)" or "micropore volume (Vp)", including reverse/list-style forms. Requirements can vary by journal or institution, so confirm the final abbreviation convention against the applicable author or thesis guidelines.

What this checks
  1. Document-type-aware definition policy. In a thesis/dissertation, use a List of Abbreviations and define each abbreviation again at first use in the Abstract and in every chapter where it appears. In journal articles, book chapters, reports, and other continuous manuscripts, follow one approach consistently: list-only use, first-use definition without a list, or list plus first-use definition.
  2. Scientific parameter notation. Method-qualified variables, derived abbreviations, and parameter symbols are accepted when the surrounding syntax clearly defines what the notation means; exact initial-letter matching is not required. Single-letter symbols are matched occurrence by occurrence so ordinary prose such as A similar procedure... is not confused with a defined variable A.
  3. Experimental identifiers. Sample, material, reactor, device, treatment, and configuration labels introduced by wording such as designated, labelled, denoted, or coded are protected as complete identifiers. Equivalent Word typography such as hyphen/en-dash variants is normalised for matching, and internal fragments such as MFC-AL within MFC-AL/AN are never treated as standalone undefined abbreviations.
  4. Instrument, product and grade names. Complete manufacturer/brand/family/model/grade phrases are detected and protected before abbreviation extraction using equipment-use context, proper-name structure, technical product lists, model codes, nearby category nouns, and manufacturer/location metadata. Commercial identifiers such as Selemion AMV, CMI-7000, or an instrument model are classified by occurrence rather than treated automatically as abbreviations. Recognition does not depend on a vendor whitelist, so unseen product grades can be handled while genuine scientific abbreviations remain subject to the normal definition rules.
  5. Nested abbreviations. A shorter acronym such as SEM may be inferred from an earlier explicit definition such as field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) when the letter-to-word mapping is exact. Because journal first-use policies vary, this is reported as a Review item rather than as a Critical error.
  6. Scholarly metadata terms. Publishing metadata labels are interpreted in context. For example, CREDIT followed by recognised author-contribution roles is treated as the CRediT Contributor Role Taxonomy rather than as an undefined scientific abbreviation.
  7. Do not use before defining. The full form must appear at or before the first use, not later.
  8. Earn the abbreviation. Defined terms that are then used only once or twice are flagged.
  9. Titles and headings excluded. The paper title and section/subsection headings, including numbered, ALL-CAPS, and Title Case headings, are not used for abbreviation-definition checks.
  10. Front matter excluded. Author/affiliation blocks, correspondence details, and Keywords/Index terms are not used for abbreviation-definition checks.
  11. Plural and possessive forms are normalised. MFCs is treated as the plural of MFC, while MFC’s performance is treated as a valid possessive use. A final uppercase letter remains part of the abbreviation, so TSS, VSS, TDS, and GIS are not shortened.
  12. Do not begin a sentence with an abbreviation.
  13. Abstract and main text are independent scopes. A definition in the Abstract does not satisfy a main-text first-use requirement. If no valid List-only convention applies, an abbreviation used in the main text must be defined according to the main-text policy even when it was already expanded in the Abstract. One equivalent definition in the Abstract and one at first use in the main text are therefore valid and are not duplicates.
  14. Abstract/main boundaries are structure-aware. Manuscript Check uses Word paragraph styles, outline levels, section numbering, Keywords/front-matter transitions, and document order to identify where the Abstract ends and the main body begins. Custom body headings are supported; the boundary is not limited to a fixed list of section names. Structured-Abstract subheadings such as Background, Methods, Results, and Conclusions are kept inside the Abstract when the document structure indicates that role.
  15. List of abbreviations. A dedicated List of Abbreviations is required by the tool's thesis/dissertation policy. For other manuscript types, a list is optional unless required by the target journal or institution. When a list is used in a continuous manuscript, list-only use and list-plus-first-use definition are both acceptable, but they must not be mixed.
  16. References are skipped by default so citations and journal acronyms do not cause false flags.
  17. Structural abbreviation scopes are independent. Word tables, table notes, figure captions, and figure legends do not participate in Abstract/main-text first-use ordering or duplicate-definition counts. Instead, each table or figure is treated as a local self-containment scope. A definition in a table note can satisfy that table, and an equivalent local definition may legitimately coexist with a main-text definition. Local definitions never satisfy main-text first use. Undefined local table/figure abbreviations are reported only as Review items because journal self-containment policies differ. Displayed equations, headers/footers, footnotes/endnotes, and References remain excluded from ordinary prose abbreviation checking.
  18. Chemical formulae are protected automatically. Valid formula notation such as KOH, NaOH, H₂SO₄, Ca(OH)₂, Fe₂(SO₄)₃, NH₄⁺, and hydrates is classified as chemical notation rather than an abbreviation. Formula fragments inside larger expressions are protected as well. Ambiguous plain capital-letter strings are excluded only when formula grammar or local chemistry evidence is strong, so genuine abbreviations such as PBS, COD, BOD, and MFC remain eligible for abbreviation checking.
  19. Definitions must establish lexical equivalence. A phrase such as humic acid (HA) is a definition, whereas measurement and condition uses such as 5.0 mg/L HA, containing 5.0 mg/L HA, with HA, or HA concentration are ordinary uses and cannot create duplicate or conflicting definitions.
  20. Duplicate and conflicting definitions are distinguished semantically. Repeating the same full form in one prose scope is reported as Defined N times, not as a conflict. Harmless variants such as electrical double-layer versus electrical double layer, capitalization, simple singular/plural variation, and selected nonessential contextual modifiers are normalized for comparison. Conflicting definitions is reserved for materially different meanings.
  21. Full-form extraction uses the nearest scientific noun phrase. Context such as reduction in charge transfer resistance (Rct) is interpreted as charge transfer resistance, rather than storing the surrounding clause as the formal descriptor.
  22. Definition tokens are reconciled before first-use checking. In artificial reef (AR), the AR token belongs to the definition event and is not simultaneously counted as an earlier ordinary use. Exact within-sentence order is still respected, so AR modules ... artificial reef (AR) remains a genuine late-definition case.
  23. Dedicated abbreviation lists are recognised globally. Definitions in recognised Abbreviations, List of Abbreviations, Acronyms, Nomenclature, or Glossary sections are retained as manuscript-level declarations. In thesis/dissertation mode, the list does not replace the required first-use definition in the Abstract or each chapter. Reintroducing the same abbreviation in a different chapter is valid and is not a duplicate. The parser supports 2-column tables and repeated column pairs such as ABBR | Full form | ABBR | Full form.
  24. Table-local definitions are handled independently. Table notes such as CE: Coulombic efficiency, CE = Coulombic efficiency, and equivalent list-style forms are recognised even when Word/publisher formatting places a footnote marker before the abbreviation. Table captions, cells, and notes do not determine main-text first use or create duplicate-definition findings; running prose is checked independently.

Reference report

The reference ledger uses context-aware bibliographic field detection. Journal articles are parsed by field order and protected spans, while books, chapters, reports, theses, standards, websites, datasets, patents, preprints, and other non-journal sources retain type-specific rules. Fields marked no are expected for that source type; n/a means the field does not apply. Ambiguous items are kept for review rather than being forced into an incompatible field pattern.

What this checks
  1. Reference ledger. Each entry is assessed for author, year, title, source, pages or article number, volume, and DOI. Word automatic numbering is recovered from DOCX list metadata before entry parsing, and terminal publisher labels such as [CrossRef] or [PubMed] do not hide reference boundaries.
  2. Style-aware applicability. Fields intentionally omitted by the dominant reference-list convention are shown as n/a rather than as errors.
  3. Reference type. Journal articles and non-journal sources are distinguished so inapplicable journal fields are not treated as required.
  4. Journal database cross-check. A secondary embedded database of 113,081 normalized full source titles and 27,100 abbreviation forms protects author/source boundaries, confirms parsed journals, and performs conservative raw-reference suffix recovery before publication year/volume tails. Missing pages or article numbers do not prevent an otherwise identifiable journal from being recognised. Entries with no abbreviation remain matchable by their full title. Database absence is not treated as an error.
  5. Ledger-only report. The References tab displays the field-status ledger without separate warning or suggestion sections.

Number, pH & precision report

How to read this report: the Numerical reporting ledger consolidates number style, pH reporting, uncertainty/range checks, p-values, and comparable precision findings in one table. Use View instances to inspect the exact manuscript context before making a change. Precision findings are limited to values inferred to be genuinely comparable.

This combines numeral usage, pH reporting, and scientific numeric-precision checks. References and headings are excluded. Word tables are checked for precision patterns only within genuinely comparable measurement columns. Precision is assessed only within comparable numeric groups, including numerical series, ranges, uncertainties, percentages, p-values, and scientific notation. The checker never invents measurement resolution or silently adds or removes significant digits; uncertain cases are flagged for author review.

What the number, pH and precision check covers
  1. Numerals vs words. Whole numbers zero to nine used as ordinary counts in prose are suggested to be spelled out; measurements, units, statistics, ratios, dates, and labels stay as numerals.
  2. pH reporting. Measured, adjusted, or target pH values should carry at least one decimal place, and directly comparable pH measurements are checked for mixed precision.
  3. Leading zeros. Decimals below one should be written as 0.5, not .5.
  4. Sentence start. Beginning a sentence with a numeral is flagged so the sentence can be restructured.
  5. Comparable precision. Decimal places or significant figures are compared only within scientifically plausible groups, not across unrelated quantities.
  6. Table-column precision. Checks consistent precision within the same parameter column.
  7. Uncertainty and ranges. A reported value and its ± variation/uncertainty should end at the same decimal place; the checker does not impose a separate significant-digit limit on the variation. Range endpoints are also checked for compatible precision.
  8. Statistics. p-values, percentages, confidence-style numerical series, and scientific notation receive conservative consistency checks.
  9. No false precision. The checker does not automatically add trailing zeros, remove justified digits, or alter standards and literature values. It flags uncertain precision for author review.

Units & notation report

Purpose: this module checks internal consistency of repeated units and their associated numerical precision. It does not force SI notation and does not compare unrelated units. Affiliations and references are excluded.

This check focuses on internal unit consistency. References and affiliations are excluded. The checker looks for meaningful inconsistencies in repeated unit notation or numerical precision; harmless exponent typography such as m2, m^2, and m² is treated as equivalent. Superscript numbers are classified from Word structure and context before unit analysis so confirmed citation or note numbers do not become part of a unit. Ambiguous superscripts are handled conservatively. The checker does not require SI notation and does not compare unrelated units.

What the units and notation check covers
  1. Unit recognition. Common scientific and environmental-engineering unit expressions are recognized as measurement units rather than abbreviations.
  2. Superscript disambiguation. A superscript number is not assumed to be a citation. Word run structure, valid unit/scientific grammar, manuscript citation style, reference numbering, mathematical context, and footnote/endnote structure are considered together. For example, the 2 in m² remains a unit exponent, while a separate superscript reference number immediately after m² is removed from the unit token when citation evidence is strong. Genuinely ambiguous cases are left unforced rather than reported as definite errors.
  3. Same-unit format. Equivalent forms such as mg/L, mg L⁻¹, and mg·L⁻¹ are recognized as the same unit; mixed use is reported only as an internal consistency issue.
  4. Same-unit precision. Repeated values for the same parameter and same unit are checked for inconsistent numerical precision, for example 10 mg/L versus 10.0 mg/L.
  5. Convention consistency. A notation is not rejected merely because it is non-SI. If one format is used consistently, it is accepted; mixed formatting of the same unit is reported.
  6. Analyte basis. Expressions such as mg N/L, mg NO3-N/L, and mg COD/L retain their analytical basis rather than being merged solely by physical dimension.
  7. Word tables. A header such as BOD (mg/L) supplies unit context to the numeric cells below it. Precision is compared only within the same parameter and unit.
  8. No automatic data edits. The checker may compare conversion factors internally but does not rewrite numerical results or invent measurement precision.

Readability & terminology report

How to read this report: this focused module checks three manuscript-specific items: sentence length, section-aware paragraph length, and terminology consistency. It does not perform grammar, spelling, punctuation, tense, pronoun/person, passive-voice, or general clarity editing. References and affiliations are excluded from the checked prose, and the Abstract is additionally excluded from paragraph-length checking.

This module intentionally avoids general grammar and language editing. It reports sentence/paragraph length indicators and manuscript-internal terminology consistency for author review.

What the readability and terminology check covers
  1. Sentence length. Prose sentences exceeding the user-selected maximum are reported for readability review. The default maximum is 35 words, and the user may select a value from 10 to 100 words.
  2. Paragraph length. Main-text narrative prose uses the user-selected minimum and maximum, with defaults of 100–300 words. The minimum remains section-aware: a short paragraph is not flagged when it is the only substantive paragraph in its local section, when the local section contains no more words than the selected minimum, when it belongs to an intentionally concise component such as a Novelty or Significance statement, when it is a genuine equation-introduction/variable-explanation paragraph directly associated with a displayed equation, or when it is a concise lead-in to a genuine bulleted/numbered list. List items themselves are excluded from paragraph-length thresholds because they are intentionally concise structural elements. The selected maximum remains paragraph-specific for narrative prose.
  3. Terminology consistency. The checker looks for repeated scientific/technical terms used in conflicting open, closed, hyphenated, or internal-capitalization forms, such as wastewater/waste water.
  4. Structural exclusions. References, affiliations, headings, captions, equations, tables, citation-like structures, headers/footers, footnotes/endnotes, and other non-prose structural content are excluded where appropriate. The Abstract is additionally excluded from paragraph-length checking.
  5. General English editing intentionally excluded. Grammar, spelling, punctuation, tense, first/second-person usage, passive voice, generic wordiness, and general clarity/conciseness checks are not performed by this module.

Figures, tables & equations report

This check uses the structure of the uploaded Word document to distinguish captions/items from ordinary cross-references. Figures, tables, equations, and supplementary items are validated as independent sequences. Placement is flagged only when the Word structure provides sufficient evidence; otherwise the report states that placement could not be verified reliably.

What the figure, table and equation check covers
  1. Independent sequences. Figures, tables, and numbered equations are checked separately, including supplementary S-numbered items.
  2. Numbering. Missing, duplicate, skipped, mixed, and out-of-order identifiers are flagged where the numbering scheme is clear.
  3. Cross-references. Grouped citations such as Figs. 2–5, Tables 1 and 2, and Eqs. (3)–(5) are expanded and checked against existing items. Figure panel citations such as Figure 2a, Figure 2c,d, and Figure 3a and S5 are resolved to their base and supplementary figures.
  4. Word caption structure. Word tabs, line breaks, split text runs, caption-number fields, and ordinary whitespace after the item number are preserved semantically. Captions such as FIGURE 2<TAB>XPS spectra..., Figure 2. XPS spectra..., and Figure 2 XPS spectra... are treated as equivalent when structural evidence supports a caption. Real embedded image objects are preferred over decorative Word shapes during figure association.
  5. Citation before appearance. Figures and tables should be cited in manuscript text before their first physical appearance. Caption text does not count as the prior citation.
  6. Equations. Equation numbers are matched locally to displayed Word math structure. In-text equation citations are then matched by identifier and document order, not by line distance, so a citation may occur many lines or a page before the displayed equation.
  7. Multipanel figures. Panel-like mentions in captions are classified as panel-label assignments or explanatory references. Only labels that assign content to panels participate in duplicate, gap, and sequence checks; references such as the inset in (d), shown in (b), or panel (c) do not create duplicate panels. Introductory structures such as SEM images of (a) sample A, (b) sample B and coordinated assignments such as (a) and (b) MSD results, EPR spectra for (d) and (e), or (f), (g), and (h) Raman spectra are treated as declared panel groups.
